chunks: Problems from too many vias. The question: What happens if you have too many vias?
Every via takes space and has a cost. A through via needs a pad on every layer and punches a clearance hole through every plane it passes. A few vias are fine.
Too many remove routing room, cut the planes into thin strips that force return currents to detour, raise the board factory's (fab's) price, and add places that can fail.
How many is too many depends on the board's density.
Punch a few holes in a paper towel and it still works as a sheet. Punch hundreds and the paper between the holes is just thin strips.
It tears easily, and anything that needs to cross it has to go around. A plane full of via holes is like that towel. It also takes the drilling machine longer, which costs money.
Area lost scales with count and with the square of antipad size. Cutting antipads from 1. 2 to 0. 8 mm saves more plane than removing a third of the vias.
This is why smaller drills and tighter antipads matter on dense boards.
Via: a plated hole connecting layers. Plane: a solid copper layer, often ground or power. Antipad: the clearance hole cut in a plane around a via that does not connect to it.
It is bigger than the drilled hole. Return path: the route a signal's current takes back to its source, usually in the plane under the trace.
Yield: the share of boards that come out of manufacturing good.
Say a 100 mm times 100 mm board has 2,000 vias, so each plane has an area of 10,000 mm². With 0. 8 mm antipads, each removes about 0.
5 mm² of copper, so 2,000 remove about 1,000 mm². That is 10% of every plane. With 1. 2 mm antipads the loss is about 23%. The antipad, not the drill, removes the copper.
If vias sit 1. 0 mm apart with 0. 9 mm antipads, the copper left between them is only 0. 1 mm wide, a narrow neck.
That is the whole idea: vias cost area, plane quality, money and reliability.

"Too many vias eat routing space because each has a pad on every layer, perforate the planes so antipads merge and break return paths, add inductive bumps on signals, raise drill cost and yield loss, and add more barrels that can fail.
I keep counts down, stagger vias so antipads don't line up, and use blind or microvias when density demands it."
